corpus_gaps: No regulations made under section 67 of the Registration of Title Act are in the corpus, so the prescribed forms and the scale of prescribed fees for inspection and certified copies under section 34 cannot be quoted.

The corpus holds the Registration of Title Act in an 'original_or_unconfirmed_consolidation' edition with no amendment_events recorded, so any post-1998 amendment to sections 13, 14, 29, 31, 34, 35 or 57 would not be visible here.

No case law or Roman-Dutch authority is in the corpus. The step that Kamal's unadjudicated prescriptive possession is not a 'title of Absolute Ownership' within section 14(a) is drawn from Prescription Ordinance section 3 alone; judicial authority on when prescriptive title vests would ordinarily be cited alongside it.

The Registration of Title Act does not define 'title of Absolute Ownership' or 'bonafide possession' (the section 75 definitions reach neither term), so the boundary between section 14(a) and section 14(b) rests on the ordinary meaning of the words.

Verifier addition: the Prescription Ordinance is amended in the corpus by the Prescription (Amendment) Act No. 26 of 2014, which replaces section 15 only; section 3 as quoted is unaffected. 'Cadastral map' is also undefined in section 75 of the Registration of Title Act, so the object of the section 34 rights is identified only by section 11 (preparation of cadastral maps).

provisions.relevant_excerpt: The Commissioner of Title Settlement shall cause an investigation to be conducted in order to determine the genuinness or otherwise of claims made in response to a Notice under section 12.
provisions.why_relevant: The question begins 'after the investigations made by the Commissioner of Title settlement'. This is the investigation stage that triggers the section 14 determination, and it fixes the officer and the moment at which the class of title is settled.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1998; no amendment events recorded in the corpus. In force at the matter reference date 2026-04.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: where the Commissioner of Title Settlement is of the view that a claimant to a land parcel has a title of Absolute Ownership, he shall declare such claimant eligible to be registered with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership
provisions.why_relevant: This is the higher class of title and the alternative that has to be ruled out before the answer can settle on a Second Class Title. It conditions the First Class declaration on the claimant having a title of Absolute Ownership, which Kamal cannot show on possession alone.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1998; no amendment events recorded in the corpus. In force at the matter reference date 2026-04.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: where the Commissioner of Title Settlement is of the view that a claimant does not qualify for a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership but the claimant is in bonafide possession of the land parcel, he may declare the claimant eligible to be registered with a Second Class Title of Ownership with the right, at the end of a period of uninterrupted and unchallenged possession of ten years from the date of registration in such capacity, to have such Second Class Title converted to a registration with First Class Title of Absolute Ownership
provisions.why_relevant: This is the operative provision for a claimant whose case rests on long possession rather than documentary title. It supplies both the class of title Kamal is eligible for and the conversion right that completes the answer.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1998; no amendment events recorded in the corpus. In force at the matter reference date 2026-04.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: A person registered with a Second Class Title of Ownership or a person claiming title through him shall at the end of a period of ten years from such registration, and if there has been no action under section 29 against such registration during the intervening period, be eligible for the conversion of his registration to one of First Class Title of Absolute Ownership.
provisions.why_relevant: Spells out the conversion right that section 14(b) refers to, and adds the condition that no section 29 action has been filed in the intervening ten years. Supports, but does not itself decide, the class Kamal is first eligible for.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1998; no amendment events recorded in the corpus. In force at the matter reference date 2026-04.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: proof of such undisturbed and uninterrupted possession as herein before explained, by such plaintiff or intervenient, or by those under whom he claims, shall entitle such plaintiff or intervenient to a decree in his favour with costs
provisions.why_relevant: The background says Kamal occupies 'by long and prescriptive rights'. This section shows what prescriptive possession does in statute: it entitles the possessor to a decree in an action. Without such a decree or any instrument of title, Kamal has no established title of Absolute Ownership to put before the Commissioner under section 14(a).
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1871; section 3 itself is unamended in the corpus. The Prescription (Amendment) Act No. 26 of 2014 amends the Ordinance but replaces section 15 only, so the text of section 3 applicable at the matter reference date 2026-04 is the text quoted.
provisions.verifier_note: Excerpt is verbatim and section 3 is unamended, but two corrections are needed: the Prescription Ordinance is amended in the corpus by the Prescription (Amendment) Act No. 26 of 2014, which replaces section 15 only, so the temporal note's 'no amendment events recorded in the corpus' is wrong at Act level though harmless for section 3; and the quoted limb stops short of the words 'by a title adverse to or independent of that of the claimant', which describe the possessor as holding a title and therefore cut against the inference the map draws from this section, so its role is reduced from indispensable support for excluding section 14(a) to context on how prescription is litigated.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: The Prescription Ordinance (Chapter 68) shall not apply to lands or interests in land registered under this Act with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership or a Second Class Title of Ownership.
provisions.why_relevant: Closes the loop on prescription: once the parcel is registered under either class, further prescriptive claims are shut out. Context for what Kamal gains on registration, not a step in choosing the class.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1998; no amendment events recorded in the corpus. In force at the matter reference date 2026-04.

provisions.relevant_excerpt: Any person aggrieved by the registration of title of a person with a Second Class Title of Ownership to any land parcel may with in a period of ten years from the date of such registration, file action for the amendment of the register, in the District Court
provisions.why_relevant: Qualifies the conversion right: the ten-year period must run unchallenged, and this is the challenge route. Explains why a Second Class Title is provisional for ten years.
provisions.temporal_note: In force from 1998; no amendment events recorded in the corpus. In force at the matter reference date 2026-04.

provisions.why_relevant: Directly answers the inspection half of the question. The right is given to 'any person', so no proprietary interest, retainer or written authority has to be shown; the only conditions are the prescribed form, the prescribed fee and office hours.

questions.authority_requirement_reason: Reclassified on verification. Sections 13 and 14 of the Registration of Title Act are verbatim in the corpus and the two classes of title and the conversion right follow from the text, but the step the answer turns on - that a claimant in possession since 1980 with no deed and no decree does not 'have a title of Absolute Ownership' within section 14(a) - cannot be taken from the corpus. The Act does not define 'title of Absolute Ownership' or 'bonafide possession' (section 75 reaches neither term), and Prescription Ordinance section 3 does not supply the step: it speaks of possession 'by a title adverse to or independent of that of the claimant', which describes the possessor as already holding a title, and it prescribes how that title is vindicated in an action rather than when it vests. Whether prescriptive title vests by operation of law after ten years or only on a decree is settled by Sri Lankan case law, which is outside this corpus, so a complete answer needs authority beyond statute.

legal_issues.issue: Whether a claimant whose only basis of claim is uninterrupted possession since 1980, without any deed, grant or court decree, has a 'title of Absolute Ownership' entitling him to be declared eligible for a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership.
Whether such a claimant is instead a person 'in bonafide possession of the land parcel' whom the Commissioner of Title Settlement may declare eligible for a Second Class Title of Ownership.
On what conditions a Second Class Title of Ownership can later be converted into a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership.

questions.hop_count_basis: Three necessary linked steps across two enactments: (1) the section 14 determination follows the section 13 investigation; (2) section 14(a) is excluded; (3) the claimant therefore falls within section 14(b). Verifier note: the hop count is left at 3 because the statutory edges are unchanged, but step (2) is not a purely statutory hop - Prescription Ordinance section 3 does not by itself exclude section 14(a), and the missing link is case law.

enrichment.original_background: Kamal Perera is in occupation in a land situated in Homagama since 1980 by long and prescriptive rights. He wants to get a title certificate to his land under the Registration of Title Act No. 21 of 1998. Kamal Perera retained Sureka Pathirana as his Notary.
enrichment.enriched_background: Kamal Perera is in occupation in a land situated in Homagama since 1980 by long and prescriptive rights. He wants to get a title certificate to his land under the Registration of Title Act No. 21 of 1998. Kamal Perera retained Sureka Pathirana as his Notary. The land he occupies is Lot 42 depicted in Cadastral Map No. HG/1247 prepared by the Surveyor-General for the Homagama title registration area, 0.1012 hectares in extent, on which Kamal built a single-storey house in 1982 and has lived with his family ever since. He went into possession in 1980 without any deed, grant, permit or other written instrument of title in his favour, he has never obtained a court decree declaring him entitled to the land, and no action about the land has ever been filed by him or against him. From 1980 to date his occupation has been open, continuous and uninterrupted, and he has paid the local authority rates for the property in his own name throughout. The order bringing the Homagama area under title registration was published in the Gazette in March 2025, the Surveyor-General issued the certified cadastral map to the Commissioner of Title Settlement in June 2025, and the Commissioner published the Gazette notice calling for claims in August 2025. Kamal submitted his claim to Lot 42 within the period allowed by that notice, no other person submitted a competing claim to Lot 42, and the Commissioner concluded his inquiry into the claim in February 2026.

added_facts.fact: The land is Lot 42 on Cadastral Map No. HG/1247 prepared by the Surveyor-General for the Homagama title registration area, 0.1012 hectares in extent, with a single-storey house Kamal built on it in 1982.
added_facts.reason: The original background identifies no parcel. The Act operates parcel by parcel on the cadastral map, so a determinate answer needs an identified land parcel. The identity chosen favours neither class of title.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: None on the outcome. A different lot number or extent would not change the class of title; it only makes the scenario capable of one determinate answer.

added_facts.fact: Kamal went into possession in 1980 without any deed, grant, permit or other written instrument of title in his favour, and has never obtained a court decree declaring him entitled to the land; no action about the land has ever been filed by him or against him.
added_facts.reason: The question turns on whether Kamal 'has a title of Absolute Ownership'. The original background says only that he occupies by 'long and prescriptive rights', which leaves open whether he also holds paper title or a prescriptive decree. This fact closes that gap.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Decisive. If Kamal held a deed of transfer or a decree declaring prescriptive title, he would have a title of Absolute Ownership and the Commissioner would declare him eligible for a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership under section 14(a), reversing the conclusion.

added_facts.fact: From 1980 to date Kamal's occupation has been open, continuous and uninterrupted; he has paid the local authority rates for the property in his own name throughout; and no other person submitted a competing claim to Lot 42 in response to the Commissioner's notice.
added_facts.reason: Section 14(b) requires the claimant to be 'in bonafide possession of the land parcel'. The original background asserts occupation but says nothing about its character or about rival claimants, so bona fide possession could not be established on the given facts.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: Decisive. If the possession had been interrupted, clandestine, or held under an acknowledgment of another's right, or if a rival claimant with paper title had come forward, the Commissioner could refuse a Second Class Title and could instead declare the rival eligible or treat the parties as co-owners.

added_facts.fact: The order bringing the Homagama area under title registration was published in the Gazette in March 2025, the Surveyor-General issued the certified cadastral map to the Commissioner of Title Settlement in June 2025, the Commissioner published the Gazette notice calling for claims in August 2025, Kamal claimed within the period allowed, and the Commissioner concluded his inquiry in February 2026.
added_facts.reason: The question is framed 'after the investigations made by the Commissioner of Title settlement', which presupposes that the area has been brought under the Act, that a cadastral map exists, that notice was published and that a claim was made in time. Supplying the sequence makes the procedural posture determinate and places it before the April 2026 reference date.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: None on the class of title. Had Kamal missed the period allowed by the notice, the question of class would not arise at all rather than be answered differently.

gold_answer_draft.issue: On the conclusion of the Commissioner of Title Settlement's investigation, which class of title is Kamal eligible to be registered with under the Registration of Title Act, given that his claim to the Homagama parcel rests only on uninterrupted possession since 1980 and he holds no deed, grant or court decree?
gold_answer_draft.rule: Under the Registration of Title Act s.13 the Commissioner of Title Settlement investigates the genuineness of claims made in answer to the notice, and s.14 requires him to publish his determination in the Gazette in one of the forms it sets out. Section 14(a) permits a declaration of eligibility for a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership only where the Commissioner is of the view that the claimant 'has a title of Absolute Ownership'. Section 14(b) provides that where a claimant does not qualify for a First Class Title but is in bonafide possession of the land parcel, the Commissioner may declare him eligible to be registered with a Second Class Title of Ownership, carrying the right, at the end of ten years of uninterrupted and unchallenged possession from the date of registration, to have that title converted into a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership. Prescription Ordinance s.3 shows how prescriptive possession works in statute: undisturbed and uninterrupted adverse possession for ten years entitles the possessor to a decree in his favour in an action. Registration of Title Act s.31(1) sets out the conversion and adds that no action under s.29 may have been filed against the registration during the ten years, and s.29(1) gives any aggrieved person that ten-year window to move the District Court. Once a parcel is registered with either class of title, s.57 excludes the Prescription Ordinance from it.
gold_answer_draft.application: Kamal's claim rests solely on his occupation since 1980. He holds no deed, grant, permit or other instrument of title, and has never obtained a decree declaring him entitled to the land; no action about the land has ever been filed. Read with Prescription Ordinance s.3, his long possession is a basis on which he could have sought a decree, not an established title of Absolute Ownership that he can put before the Commissioner. He therefore does not satisfy s.14(a). His position does answer to s.14(b): his occupation of Lot 42 has been open, continuous and uninterrupted for more than forty years, he has paid the local authority rates in his own name throughout, he built and lives in a house on the parcel, and no competing claim to Lot 42 was submitted in answer to the Commissioner's notice. On those facts the Commissioner can properly take the view that Kamal is in bonafide possession of the parcel although he does not qualify for a First Class Title.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Kamal is eligible to be declared, in the Commissioner's Gazette determination, eligible for registration with a Second Class Title of Ownership under s.14(b), not with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership under s.14(a). That Second Class Title carries the right, after ten years of uninterrupted and unchallenged possession from the date of registration and provided no action under s.29 has been filed in that period, to be converted under s.31 into a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership; on registration under either class the Prescription Ordinance ceases to apply to the parcel by s.57. Two qualifications should be stated. Section 14(b) is permissive ('may'), so the declaration rests on the view the Commissioner forms on the investigation, and the Act does not define 'title of Absolute Ownership', so a claimant who could produce a decree or an instrument of title would be assessed under s.14(a) instead.

answer_claims.claim_text: On the conclusion of the investigation under s.13, the Commissioner of Title Settlement must publish his determination in the Gazette in one of the forms set out in s.14.
A claimant may be declared eligible for a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership only where the Commissioner is of the view that the claimant has a title of Absolute Ownership.
A claimant who does not qualify for a First Class Title but who is in bonafide possession of the land parcel may be declared eligible for a Second Class Title of Ownership.

Under Prescription Ordinance s.3, undisturbed and uninterrupted adverse possession for ten years entitles the possessor to a decree in his favour in an action; the Ordinance provides for a decree rather than a self-executing documentary title.

A Second Class Title of Ownership carries a right of conversion into a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership at the end of ten years of uninterrupted and unchallenged possession from registration, provided no action under s.29 was filed in that period.
Once a parcel is registered with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership or a Second Class Title of Ownership, the Prescription Ordinance no longer applies to it.

Kamal holds no deed, grant, permit or other instrument of title and has never obtained a decree declaring him entitled to the land, so he cannot show the Commissioner a title of Absolute Ownership within s.14(a).

Kamal's open, continuous and uninterrupted occupation of Lot 42 since 1980, with rates paid in his own name and no competing claim submitted in answer to the notice, supports the view that he is in bonafide possession of the land parcel.
Kamal is eligible to be declared eligible for registration with a Second Class Title of Ownership, not a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership.

After ten years of uninterrupted and unchallenged possession from that registration, and if no action under s.29 has been filed in the meantime, Kamal becomes eligible for conversion of his registration to a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership.
The declaration under s.14(b) is permissive and depends on the view the Commissioner forms on the investigation, so the class of title is not automatic.

questions.block_reason: Reserved by the verifier. The conclusion that Kamal falls outside section 14(a) and inside section 14(b) rests on an inference about the effect of prescriptive possession that no provision in the corpus states, and that Prescription Ordinance section 3 arguably contradicts on its own words. Nothing turns on agency, on the Notary's retainer or on any non-statutory doctrine, so a complete answer follows from the corpus text alone.

A title register for that area is kept by the Registrar of Title at the Homagama Title Registry, and the cadastral map used for registration of title in the area is held by the Superintendent of Surveys for the Colombo District. Sureka wishes to attend at the Homagama Title Registry during office hours to examine the folio relating to Lot 42 and to examine the cadastral map, and she also wants to place on her file a certified extract of the folio and a certified copy of an extract of the cadastral map. The scenario needs an identified parcel and an identified custodian of each document for the answer to be determinate.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: If no title register or cadastral map were yet maintained for the area under the Act, there would be nothing to inspect and s.34 would not be engaged.

added_facts.reason: The question asks whether she may act 'on behalf of' Kamal. Whether she needs authority is the point in issue, so the scenario must state whether she has any. It also has to state her willingness to meet the form and fee conditions, which are the only statutory conditions.
added_facts.counterfactual_effect: None on the outcome, and that is the point: because s.34 confers the right on 'any person', the absence of written authority does not defeat it. If instead she declined to apply on the prescribed form or to pay the prescribed fee, the statutory conditions would not be met and neither inspection nor certified copies could be demanded.

gold_answer_draft.issue: Whether Sureka, a Notary holding no written authority from Kamal, may inspect the title register and the cadastral map maintained under the Registration of Title Act, and whether she is entitled to certified copies of those documents and from whom.
gold_answer_draft.rule: Registration of Title Act s.34(1) provides that any person may, on application made in the prescribed form and on payment of the prescribed fee, inspect during office hours any title register and any cadastral map maintained under the Act. Section 34(2) entitles any person, on application made to the relevant Registrar of Title and on payment of the prescribed fee, to receive an extract of the Title Register certified by that Registrar of Title. Section 34(3) entitles any person, on application made to the relevant Superintendent of Surveys and on payment of the prescribed fee, to receive a copy of an extract of the cadastral map used for registration of title, certified on behalf of the Surveyor-General. Section 75 defines 'Registrar of Title' as any person appointed as such under the Act, 'Superintendent of Surveys' as any person performing those functions in the Survey Department, and 'Title Register' as the register under the Act, which fixes who the two custodians are. The forms and fees referred to are those prescribed by regulations made under s.67(2)(g) and (h). By s.35(1) a document purporting to be certified by a Registrar of Title is presumed to have been so certified and is accepted as prima facie evidence of the matter to which it relates without further proof.
gold_answer_draft.application: Section 34 confers each of these rights on 'any person'. It does not require the applicant to be the owner, a claimant, or the agent of one, and it calls for no proof of interest or written authority. Sureka is a person within s.34, so the fact that Kamal has given her no written authority or power of attorney, and that she is not herself a claimant to Lot 42, does not stand in her way; she may apply whether or not she is described as acting for Kamal. What she must do is apply in the prescribed form, pay the prescribed fee and attend during office hours, all of which she is willing to do. For the certified extract of the register relating to Lot 42 she must apply to the relevant Registrar of Title, that is the Registrar at the Homagama Title Registry, who certifies it. For the certified copy of an extract of the cadastral map she must apply not to that Registrar but to the relevant Superintendent of Surveys, here the Superintendent of Surveys for the Colombo District, and the copy is certified on behalf of the Surveyor-General.
gold_answer_draft.conclusion: Yes on both counts. Sureka may inspect the title register and the cadastral map under s.34(1) on application in the prescribed form, payment of the prescribed fee and during office hours, and she needs no authority from Kamal because the right belongs to any person. She is also entitled to certified copies, but from two different officers: a certified extract of the Title Register from the relevant Registrar of Title under s.34(2), and a certified copy of an extract of the cadastral map from the relevant Superintendent of Surveys, certified on behalf of the Surveyor-General, under s.34(3). Each is subject to payment of the prescribed fee. A certified document of the first kind is prima facie evidence of what it relates to under s.35. The prescribed forms and the amounts of the fees are set by regulations, which are not reproduced here.

answer_claims.claim_text: Any person may, on application in the prescribed form and on payment of the prescribed fee, inspect during office hours any title register and any cadastral map maintained under the Registration of Title Act.
Any person is entitled, on application to the relevant Registrar of Title and payment of the prescribed fee, to an extract of the Title Register certified by that Registrar of Title.
A certified copy of an extract of the cadastral map is obtained from the relevant Superintendent of Surveys and is certified on behalf of the Surveyor-General, not by the Registrar of Title.
The forms and fees to which s.34 refers are those prescribed by regulations made under the Act.
A document purporting to be certified by a Registrar of Title is presumed to have been so certified and is accepted as prima facie evidence of the matter to which it relates without further proof.

Sureka is a person within s.34, and because the section requires no proof of interest or written authority, the absence of any authority or power of attorney from Kamal does not prevent her from inspecting or from obtaining certified copies.
She must apply on the prescribed form, pay the prescribed fee and attend during office hours, and she is willing to meet those conditions.

The certified extract of the register for Lot 42 must be sought from the Registrar of Title at the Homagama Title Registry, and the certified copy of an extract of the cadastral map from the Superintendent of Surveys for the Colombo District.
Sureka may inspect both the title register and the cadastral map on behalf of Kamal, and could equally do so in her own name.
She may also obtain certified copies of both documents, but from two different officers and on payment of the prescribed fee in each case.
